items.title: Nvidia has no chief compliance officer. Its board now faces an oversight test
items.summary:
Good morning. Nvidia’s sudden leadership shake-up raises a bigger question than who will replace Jensen Huang: Did the company’s board do enough to ensure its export-control rules were working, and what should investors expect it to do now?

With CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO following Huang’s resignation last week, the board, now chaired by Harvey Jones , must choose a permanent leader and assess whether the company’s compliance safeguards worked.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance practices Sunday, questioning whether potential violations of U.S. export restrictions were isolated or involved senior management. “Was it a low-level fail? Was it in the middle or was it up in the C-suite? And who knew?” he asked on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures .

The controversy is further complicated by reports of an affair between Huang and Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based Nvidia business partner. Huang has acknowledged infidelity but has not publicly identified the woman.

The central export-control question is whether advanced Nvidia chips supplied through Megaspeed were diverted to China. U.S. rules have permitted certain data centers outside China to provide remote computing services to Chinese customers, but that is distinct from the unauthorized transfer of restricted physical chips, Fortune reported .

U.S. authorities have also reportedly examined Alice Huang’s possible connections to Chinese intelligence. Those allegations remain unproven, and investigations into Megaspeed’s…
items.t: Nvidia has no chief compliance officer. Its board now faces an oversight test

items.title: Gen Z and millennials will make up half of holiday spending just in time for the great consumer tradedown
items.summary:
American shoppers are hunting for cheaper stores harder than at any point since the pandemic-throttled period of early 2021, according to Bank of America card data . By BofA’s measure, they’re trading down more now than at any point since 2022, including June of that year, when inflation peaked at 9.1% , the biggest jump in more than 40 years.

It should make for a particularly diminished holiday spending season, as millennials and Gen Z come of age in the economy of the 2020s. The two cohorts now account for 50% of holiday spending, a first in Deloitte’s annual holiday survey , and both groups are planning double-digit increases this year. 

At the same time, BofA finds that since 2022, millennials have been trading down faster than Gen X or baby boomers, particularly in apparel and groceries, “suggesting greater sensitivity to rising costs.” Apparel shows some of the clearest trading down overall, and the bank said some households may be putting off clothing purchases and “shopping closer to need.” 

BofA Institute’s Spending Tier Composite, built from card and deposit data on apparel, dining, groceries and travel, tracks how much spending goes to value-tier merchants. It “suggests consumers are trading down at the highest level since 2021,” the bank wrote Nov. 9. “Rather than spending less, many appear to be changing where – and how – they spend.”

Bank of America Institute’s Spending Tier Composite (red, right axis), a proxy for trading down in which lower readings mean more spending at value-tier merchants, plotted against the Conference Board Consumer Confidence…
items.t: Gen Z and millennials will make up half of holiday spending just in time for the great consumer tradedown

items.title: Most work doesn’t need the Ferrari of AI, Wharton and Accenture find, but companies may be paying for it anyway
items.summary:
When companies unleash AI agents, they like to reach for the shiniest, newest, and most powerful model and use it for every job task. A new joint report from the Wharton School and Accenture published Monday suggests that might be overkill.

The landmark new report , What Does Agentic AI Really Cost? , studied more than 18,000 tasks and work activities across 923 occupations. More than 90% of tasks in the framework that AI agents could take over are routine enough for the less expensive models. Moreover, in each of the 19 industries studied, only 6% to 11% of the work AI agents could do is complex enough to typically need a bleeding edge “frontier” model, according to the research findings. Meaning, complex tasks that need frontier models are a small portion of the workflow. 

Yet, Eric Bradlow, vice dean of AI and analytics at Wharton and a coauthor of the report, said he doubts most companies are making that distinction. 

“I don’t even think most companies are thinking about deploying differential models for different parts of the workflow,” Bradlow told Fortune . “I think they’re taking possibly their most sophisticated model and applying it to all of the workflow.”

That may not deliver the best return, he said, “because certain tasks, a large fraction of tasks, just do not require the more sophisticated models.”

Chasing Shiny Objects 

Bradlow said people often seek out the latest—and usually marketed as the greatest—model. 

“Most people tend to want to have, I’ll call it the shiniest object,” he said. “But for most tasks, actually, you don’t.”

To reach their…
items.t: Most work doesn’t need the Ferrari of AI, Wharton and Accenture find, but companies may be paying for it anyway

items.title: McKinsey Global Institute: Trade’s $4 trillion Achilles’ heel is also an opportunity
items.summary:
On Nov. 6, the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency announced up to $2 billion to buy strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile. DLA aims to create targeted demand signals to enable domestic production. In fact, the United States produces a small fraction of many of the critical minerals it uses, including less than 1% of the most common type of rare-earth magnet it uses. In other words, these products are among America’s “Achilles’ Heels.”

The global market for solving these vulnerabilities is huge. More than $4 trillion of global imports, nearly a quarter of the total, sit in what our new research calls the Achilles’ heel of global trade: products that face at least two of three vulnerabilities. They are critical to economic activity, they come from a handful of suppliers, or they come from geopolitically distant partners. For business, they can also be a map of where the next growth opportunities lie.

Companies are moving, for example by finding ways to have alternative sources of rare earths outside of China and by pooling purchasing commitments for generic drugs. Software companies now sell visibility into suppliers several tiers upstream.

The next era of globalization is not about retreat; it is about reconfiguration. In 2025, U.S.–China goods trade fell nearly 30%, yet total U.S. imports and Chinese exports reached new highs, and trade is now traveling shorter geopolitical distances as economies shift toward more closely aligned partners. So businesses need to understand where that reconfiguration is most likely to happen, and much of it could…
items.t: McKinsey Global Institute: Trade’s $4 trillion Achilles’ heel is also an opportunity

items.title: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind
items.summary:
Artificial intelligence promises to untangle the messy workflows that have long plagued legacy industries. One startup is bringing that pitch to car dealerships. On Monday, Oakland-based company Numa announced a $45 million Series C round to build out an AI operating system designed to handle the daily grind of dealership customer service, from answering calls and booking appointments to keeping customers updated on their cars. 

It works like this: Numa’s AI agents connect to a dealership’s software to check inventory down to a car’s trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review.

“Think about things like filling out warranty paperwork. That is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do, and people do it poorly. You can apply an AI and do it instantly,” Numa CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune .

Blue Cloud Ventures led the round, bringing Numa’s total funding to $91 million. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa Ventures, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, Mitsui and Tokio Marine also participated. Founded in 2017, Numa previously raised seed and Series A funding from investors including Draper Fisher Jurvetson. The latest round valued Numa at $500 million after the investment, according to a source familiar with the company.

Numa’s pitch comes as more companies put AI agents to work. In a survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare,…
items.t: AI startup Numa raises $45 million to help car dealerships leave the paperwork behind

items.title: At Cantor’s crypto summit, a window into Tether’s ambitions and a warning on cyberattacks
items.summary:
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong once sent an executive from San Francisco to New York with the goal of making inroads with the storied Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald. It did not go well. Arriving alone, the executive recalls he was greeted by Cantor’s then-CEO Howard Lutnick and a dozen lieutenants, who ridiculed his General Manager title: “So I sat down with this big, sharp-elbowed financial company, trying to work a deal…The CEO laughs at me and goes ‘Hey GM, are you going to make my coffee?’ I came out to New York and got my ass handed to me by old-school traders.”

That anecdote, which I recount in my history of Coinbase’s early years, took place in 2016. A decade later, things are a little different. In Miami last week, Lutnick’s son Brandon presided over Cantor Converge, an annual summit dedicated to blockchain and other new technology—where this year’s keynote speaker was none other than Brian Armstrong.

I sat down with the younger Lutnick, whose dress and appearance are every inch that of a Wall Street banker, but who speaks fluent crypto. He revealed that he is bullish about four parts of the sector in particular: Bitcoin, stablecoins, remittances, and exchanges like Coinbase that are crypto native but now offer everything from tokenized equities to prediction markets.

In the long term, I suspect he’s correct on all four counts. But it is his and Cantor’s ties to stablecoins, and in particular Tether, that are most intriguing. Those include an arrangement that saw Cantor become the custodian for Tether’s massive reserves, receiving a small stake of the…
items.t: At Cantor’s crypto summit, a window into Tether’s ambitions and a warning on cyberattacks

items.title: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients
items.summary:
The Kritzberger family has farmed in the Red River Valley for more than a century. They once had livestock. Now they grow sugar beets, soybeans, and grains.

Like many farmers, they labor to balance the books. “We’re in an incredible amount of debt,” Ang Kritzberger said as she walked the farm on a recent fall morning.

For the past 10 years, the Kritzbergers have had another worry. Their daughter Nina has Type 1 diabetes. That’s landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs.

Nina was diagnosed when she was 7.

“I slept by her bedside for the first 60 days,” Ang Kritzberger said. “And I had to stick her finger every two hours, 24 hours a day, to make sure that she was OK.”

The Kritzbergers also pay a lot out-of-pocket every year for medical care, despite having insurance — at least $8,000 for drugs, supplies, and medical appointments.

That’s not uncommon. Soaring insulin prices for years forced people with diabetes to pay hundreds, even thousands, of dollars. Many rationed insulin, with sometimes deadly consequences.

But today, there’s a growing movement across the country to cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin. That’s brought together Democrats and Republicans, tapping an emerging consensus that the government should protect people from high drug prices.

“Typically, Republicans are more on the free-market side of things, Democrats are more supportive of intervening,” said North Dakota state Sen. Sean Cleary, a Republican. “But in this case, I think there was broad-enough agreement that this market just wasn’t…
items.t: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients

items.title: Who inherits Jensen Huang’s empire? The Nvidia CEO contenders facing an extraordinary test
items.summary:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spent more than three decades building an enterprise whose technological ambitions, commercial relationships, and very identity became inseparable from his leadership. 

Yet for a company that demonstrated extraordinary foresight in anticipating the future of computing, the absence of a deep internal bench capable of succeeding its founder raises uncomfortable questions about the board’s long-term stewardship.

With longtime CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO, attention has turned to an eclectic field of potential outside successors. Their varied credentials underscore just how difficult it will be to replace a leader whose influence permeated virtually every dimension of the business.

Fortune senior writer Sheryl Estrada examined the potential contenders , finding an array of accomplished executives whose qualifications are matched by significant questions about their suitability—or willingness—to take the helm.

Arm CEO Rene Haas offers perhaps the closest connection to Nvidia’s foundations. He spent seven years at the company, understands its culture, and now leads a business whose architecture underpins Nvidia’s Grace and Vera CPUs. But Haas left in 2013, before Nvidia’s ascent to AI dominance, and would be returning to an enterprise vastly more complex than the one he knew.

Another option is AMD CEO Lisa Su, who brings formidable semiconductor credentials and a proven record of corporate transformation. Since 2014, she has rebuilt AMD into a major force in processors and an increasingly credible challenger in AI chips. Her…
items.t: Who inherits Jensen Huang’s empire? The Nvidia CEO contenders facing an extraordinary test

items.title: VC Bradley Tusk decided to offer startups services instead of cash. How’s that working out?
items.summary:
Good morning, it’s Finance Editor Jeff Roberts in for Allie. In the course of my career, I’ve interviewed hundreds of venture capitalists, and I have an observation: Many VCs regard themselves as unconventional thinkers, but when it comes to the norms of their industry, they are highly conformist. Bradley Tusk is not one of those VCs.

Brash and outspoken, Tusk made his name as the chief of staff for former New York City mayor Mike Bloomberg, and by helping Uber in its early battles with city officials and the taxi industry. Soon after, he leveraged his reputation as a political fixer to launch Tusk Ventures, which helped startups like Lemonade, Bird, FanDuel, Ro, and Coinbase navigate various regulatory minefields.

In 2025, Tusk made another bold bet. Despite a successful run as a conventional VC, which saw Tusk raise $300 million over three funds, he decided to abandon the model in favor of something novel: taking equity in exchange for services rather than cash. 

“I took half a step back and asked, ‘What do I and don’t I like about this process?’ I like two things: I like legalizing disruptive shit, and I like betting on and working with founders who are interesting. What I did not like was raising money, dealing with LPs, taking board seats, and portfolio construction. I also didn’t like giving someone else 80% of my profits,” Tusk explains.

In practice, Tusk says the pivot means his firm spends almost all of its time on a few core areas. Those include helping startups obtain licenses and navigate regulations, and turning up on fundraising calls to assure would-be…
items.t: VC Bradley Tusk decided to offer startups services instead of cash. How’s that working out?

items.title: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost
items.summary:
Currencies such as the Japanese yen or the euro have tried and failed to loosen the U.S. dollar’s grip on world trade , unable to outweigh the U.S.’s deep and open financial markets. But now, Japanese bankers think that the rise of digital currencies could give the yen a new path to worldwide use.

“The currency competition is now a software competition,” Tomoya Hasebe, global head of digital and innovation at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), said at a roundtable organized by FinCity Tokyo in Singapore on Nov. 16. “Currency dominance is increasingly determined not only by central bank policy or regulatory policy, but by which currency is easiest to use as code.” 

The yen is the world’s third most-used currency, after the U.S. dollar and the euro.

Japan was the first country among G7 economies to roll out a comprehensive framework to regulate stablecoins. Yet yen-pegged stablecoins have barely enjoyed much usage, with U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins accounting for more than 97% of the market .

The country’s three megabanks— Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, and the Mizuho Financial Group—are planning to change that with a jointly-issued yen-backed stablecoin set to begin transactions next March . The new stablecoin is meant to streamline cross-border payments and boost the appeal of the yen for global business.

Several Asian economies are rolling out their own stablecoins to cater to firms seeking alternatives to the U.S. dollar. Hong Kong, for example, issued its first two Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin issuer licenses…
items.t: ‘The currency competition is now a software competition’: Why Japan’s banks think digital currencies give the yen a boost

items.title: Who’s duping whom? Cut-price versions of luxury items are Christmas hit
items.summary:
From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cheaper dupes of high-end goods have gone mainstream. But is it fair?

For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries.

But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.

items.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
items.summary:
Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised

Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.”

In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn, announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social…
items.t: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.

items.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
items.summary:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.
